info.text: Interactive check questions for Lesson 4.3: LLM-Assisted Transcription: Hallucination, Bias, and the Specialization Gap.

questiontext.text: What is the primary objective of comparing manual, specialized HTR, and vision-language model transcriptions today?

generalfeedback.text: The question is not which system is best but what kind of error each makes — the kinds differ more than the rates.

answer.text: To understand what each kind of system does and what its characteristic failure modes reveal about its underlying architecture.

feedback.text: Correct. The differences in error types — conspicuous letter sequences vs. fluent invented Greek — matter far more to a scholarly editor than simple aggregate error rates.

answer.text: To declare a single permanent software winner that will replace all human transcribers for the remainder of the course.

feedback.text: Incorrect. The goal is evaluating different tools against specific material rather than picking a universal winner.

answer.text: To test whether vision-language models can automatically grade student assignments without instructor oversight.

feedback.text: Incorrect. The focus is diplomatic transcription and error characterization on historical manuscripts.

answer.text: To prove that computer vision algorithms should never be applied to humanities research.

feedback.text: Incorrect. The exercise establishes where each tool is viable and where it fails.

name.text: 02 Question: What a Vision-Language Model Is

questiontext.text: Why does a vision-language model's extensive linguistic knowledge become a liability when transcribing historical manuscripts?

generalfeedback.text: A VLM's linguistic knowledge is its strength on modern text and its liability on manuscripts, because it resolves ambiguous ink by expectation.

answer.text: It resolves ambiguous or damaged visual evidence by applying its statistical expectation of language, leading to fluent inventions rather than faithful diplomatic records.

feedback.text: Correct. A diplomatic transcription must record the physical ink as written, whereas a VLM's language model tends to complete text based on plausible expectation.

answer.text: Its linguistic knowledge slows down token generation speeds on GPU servers.

feedback.text: Incorrect. Generation speed is high; the liability is cognitive and evidential distortion.

answer.text: It forces the model to reject any image containing Greek polytonic diacritics.

feedback.text: Incorrect. The model attempts to transcribe Greek, but it over-applies linguistic priors to ambiguous ink.

answer.text: It causes the model to automatically delete the TEI header from the repository.

feedback.text: Incorrect. The issue is text generation behaviour during zero-shot transcription.

questiontext.text: What empirical finding demonstrates that the specialization gap in vision-language models is driven by historical period rather than language?

generalfeedback.text: The same model achieves 1.39% CER on modern handwriting and 52.23% on historical — the gap is period, not language.

answer.text: The same model (GPT-4o) achieved 1.39% CER on modern English handwriting but 52.23% CER on historical English handwriting from the Bentham corpus.

feedback.text: Correct. The fortyfold performance degradation occurs on the same language, proving that lack of exposure to historical scripts and conventions is the root cause.

answer.text: Models perform identically on modern and medieval Latin texts regardless of parameter scale.

feedback.text: Incorrect. On medieval Latin, general commercial models produced 63–84% CER compared to 14.6% for domain-tuned models.

answer.text: Vision-language models achieve 0.00% Word Error Rate on all 18th-century German manuscripts.

feedback.text: Incorrect. Models reached ~97% WER on historical German, indicating complete failure.

answer.text: English manuscripts show no performance difference across eight centuries of transmission.

feedback.text: Incorrect. Historical English showed a drastic jump in error rate compared to modern English.

questiontext.text: What is 'over-historicization' in the context of vision-language model transcription?

generalfeedback.text: GPT-4o beat a generic HTR baseline on CER while inventing anachronistic characters in 59% of files — the metric and the fidelity diverge.

answer.text: The algorithmic insertion of archaic characters or graphemes from an earlier historical epoch that are not present in the source manuscript.

feedback.text: Correct. The model associates 'old document' with archaic orthography and hallucinates obsolete characters (e.g. pre-Petrine Cyrillic in 18th-century texts).

answer.text: The tendency of human historians to overestimate the age of a manuscript based on watermarks.

feedback.text: Incorrect. Over-historicization is an algorithmic hallucination of archaic characters by AI models.

answer.text: The automatic removal of all historical punctuation by modern OCR software.

feedback.text: Incorrect. That is silent modernization; over-historicization is the insertion of anachronistic archaic characters.

answer.text: A database error that overwrites manuscript creation dates with random timestamps.

feedback.text: Incorrect. It is a specific generative hallucination phenomenon in historical OCR/HTR.

name.text: 05 Question: Why CER Is Insufficient for Historical Text

questiontext.text: Why do researchers use supplementary metrics like Historical Character Preservation Rate (HCPR) and Archaic Insertion Rate (AIR) alongside CER?

generalfeedback.text: A model can score well on CER while silently modernizing or hallucinating archaism — check preservation and insertion separately.

answer.text: Because a model can achieve a deceptively low CER while systematically destroying diplomatic fidelity through silent modernization or hallucinated archaisms.

feedback.text: Correct. CER treats all character substitutions identically, failing to distinguish harmless minor typos from severe temporal or orthographic corruption.

answer.text: CER can only be computed for Latin characters, requiring HCPR for Greek and Cyrillic.

feedback.text: Incorrect. CER is calculated on any script; HCPR and AIR measure specific qualitative historical fidelity.

answer.text: Because CER requires manual double-keying by three independent certified archivists.

feedback.text: Incorrect. CER is an automated Levenshtein edit distance; HCPR/AIR measure historical preservation specifically.

answer.text: Because international copyright registries reject papers that report standard CER.

feedback.text: Incorrect. The justification is philological and methodological rigor.

questiontext.text: What is the consequence of a vision-language model reflowing transcribed text as continuous prose rather than preserving line breaks?

generalfeedback.text: VLMs reflow lines, add commentary, and fill gaps confidently — none of which announces itself in the output.

answer.text: The output cannot be aligned to facsimile image zones, cannot be used for line-level HTR training, and prevents direct line-by-line error comparison.

feedback.text: Correct. Preserving manuscript line breaks is structural; without them, image-text bindings and granular verification collapse.

answer.text: The output is automatically encrypted and locked by the API server.

feedback.text: Incorrect. The text is readable prose, but structurally detached from the physical manuscript layout.

answer.text: Continuous prose causes web browsers to display the text in reverse character order.

feedback.text: Incorrect. Text displays normally, but cannot link to line zones or serve as line training data.

answer.text: Reflowing text reduces the token cost of the API call by 90%.

feedback.text: Incorrect. API token cost is based on prompt and output token count, not line break count.

questiontext.text: Why must you record the exact prompt verbatim, model version, and access date when running transcription experiments with hosted VLMs?

generalfeedback.text: Record the prompt verbatim, the model version, and the date — without them the result is not reproducible.

answer.text: Hosted models are updated without notice and respond differently to slight prompt variations, making full documentation essential for scientific reproducibility.

feedback.text: Correct. A reported error rate without exact prompt, version, and date cannot be verified or replicated by future researchers.

answer.text: Commercial API providers require this metadata to issue academic research grants.

feedback.text: Incorrect. Provenance documentation is a standard scholarly reproducibility requirement.

answer.text: Recording the date prevents the model from generating conversational framing text.

feedback.text: Incorrect. Prompt constraints reduce conversational filler; recording metadata ensures reproducibility.

answer.text: The TEI schema rejects XML documents unless the model access date is validated via RelaxNG.

feedback.text: Incorrect. TEI schemas validate document structure, while metadata records experimental provenance.

questiontext.text: Why does a good transcription prompt include explicit constraints against modernizing, expanding abbreviations, and filling gaps?

generalfeedback.text: Every constraint in the prompt addresses a documented failure mode, and a good prompt reduces those failures without eliminating them.

answer.text: Each constraint addresses a documented default failure mode of general-purpose models, reducing unwanted generative intervention.

feedback.text: Correct. Without explicit constraints, models default to conversational prose, expanded abbreviations, normalized spelling, and silent gap filling.

answer.text: Adding negative constraints guarantees 0% character error rate on all Greek minuscule texts.

feedback.text: Incorrect. Constraints reduce but do not eliminate hallucination and formatting failures; verification is still required.

answer.text: Negative constraints reduce the memory consumption of the vision transformer during image tokenization.

feedback.text: Incorrect. Prompt text guides autoregressive decoding; it does not reduce vision transformer patch memory.

answer.text: Prompts without negative constraints are automatically rejected by LLM safety classifiers.

feedback.text: Incorrect. Prompts without constraints simply produce unconstrained, normalized, or conversational output.

questiontext.text: Why must you save and commit the raw, unedited output of the VLM before making any corrections or reformatting?

generalfeedback.text: Commit the raw output before correcting or reformatting anything — that state is what Week 5 measures.

answer.text: The raw output represents the exact empirical state that must be measured and scored against the ground truth in Week 5.

feedback.text: Correct. Correcting or reformatting raw output prior to committing destroys the measurement baseline and obscures true model performance.

answer.text: Git will corrupt the repository history if a machine-generated file is edited before its initial commit.

feedback.text: Incorrect. Git tracks whatever text is committed; preserving raw output is an experimental discipline.

answer.text: To ensure that the API provider does not charge for tokens generated during human post-editing.

feedback.text: Incorrect. Token billing occurs during the API call, regardless of local Git operations.

answer.text: Raw commits are automatically converted into TEI apparatus entries by GitHub Actions.

feedback.text: Incorrect. Preserving raw commits provides the audit baseline for error analysis.

questiontext.text: Why can you not evaluate the accuracy of a VLM transcription simply by reading through the generated text?

generalfeedback.text: Fluent output reads as correct, so check against the image — and look specifically at where you recorded damage.

answer.text: The model produces fluent, grammatically correct text that reads perfectly while potentially disagreeing completely with the actual ink on the parchment.

feedback.text: Correct. Plausible wrong words and fabricated readings cannot be detected by reading the prose; they can only be identified by comparing against the image at full zoom.

answer.text: VLM outputs are written in an encrypted dialect of Greek that only neural networks can parse.

feedback.text: Incorrect. The output is standard Greek text, which is deceptively fluent.

answer.text: Reading VLM text causes transcribers to lose their active Git session credentials.

feedback.text: Incorrect. The risk is cognitive confirmation bias and accepting plausible hallucinations.

answer.text: Reading without an automated XML parser triggers fatal syntax exceptions in the terminal.

feedback.text: Incorrect. Text reading is a human cognitive task; image verification is required.

questiontext.text: What is the methodological implication of finding that a VLM's self-reported uncertainty markers (e.g. [?]) do not correlate with its actual errors?

generalfeedback.text: If the model's uncertainty markers do not track its errors, you must check everything — and the tool saves no verification labour at all.

answer.text: You cannot rely on uncertainty markers to direct your review, meaning you must check every single word against the image and save no verification labour.

feedback.text: Correct. Poor calibration means the tool provides no selective reduction in human verification effort.

answer.text: The model should immediately be retrained with a higher temperature parameter.

feedback.text: Incorrect. Raising temperature increases randomness and hallucination; poor calibration is an inherent model property.

answer.text: The transcriber should automatically delete all lines containing question marks.

feedback.text: Incorrect. Unreliable markers mean all lines must be checked against the manuscript image.

answer.text: Transkribus credits can be refunded by submitting the miscalibrated output to customer support.

feedback.text: Incorrect. LLM uncertainty calibration is an active research challenge, not a billing defect.

questiontext.text: How can an editor determine whether a vision-language model is actually reading the manuscript image or reciting a well-known text from memory?

generalfeedback.text: Where your manuscript differs from the printed text, a model reciting from memory gives the printed reading — that is the test.

answer.text: Check what the model outputs at known manuscript variant readings and in physically damaged lacunae.

feedback.text: Correct. If the model outputs the standard printed text where the witness has a variant, or fills a damaged lacuna fluently, it is reciting from training memory.

answer.text: Prompt the model to state its training dataset copyright licenses.

feedback.text: Incorrect. Models cannot provide reliable internal data provenance via zero-shot prompts.

answer.text: Measure the inference latency in milliseconds between consecutive output tokens.

feedback.text: Incorrect. Token generation speed does not distinguish image attention from memory retrieval.

answer.text: Check whether the output contains modern English punctuation marks.

feedback.text: Incorrect. Punctuation reflects prompt adherence; variant readings and lacunae test reading vs. memorization.

name.text: 13 Question: Computing a Preliminary Error Rate

questiontext.text: Why must both the reference ground truth and the hypothesis text be normalized to Unicode NFC before computing Character Error Rate?

generalfeedback.text: Normalize both strings to NFC before computing CER, or you measure encoding difference rather than transcription difference.

answer.text: If one string is NFC (precomposed) and the other is NFD (decomposed), Levenshtein distance will compare byte sequences and grossly inflate the error rate despite identical visual text.

feedback.text: Correct. Normalizing both strings ensures you measure true transcription differences rather than character composition encoding differences.

answer.text: Python's unicodedata module cannot process Greek polytonic characters in NFD format.

feedback.text: Incorrect. Python handles both, but comparing NFC against NFD computes character edit mismatches on identical graphemes.

answer.text: NFC normalization automatically translates medieval abbreviations into modern Greek.

feedback.text: Incorrect. Unicode normalization standardizes code point representation; it does not alter lexical content.

answer.text: Git merge tools will corrupt files that contain NFC-normalized polytonic vowels.

feedback.text: Incorrect. NFC is the standard canonical normalization form recommended across the pipeline.

name.text: 14 Question: Where LLMs Are Genuinely Useful

questiontext.text: What general principle distinguishes the tasks where LLMs are genuinely effective in textual scholarship from those where they fail?

generalfeedback.text: These tools help where linguistic knowledge is the point and harm where it contaminates evidence — transcription is the second kind.

answer.text: They succeed at tasks where broad linguistic knowledge is the goal (translation, explaining palaeography, code drafting) and fail where linguistic priors contaminate historical evidence (diplomatic transcription).

feedback.text: Correct. Linguistic priors help in synthesis and language tasks, but corrupt diplomatic transcription by imposing statistical expectations onto unique artifacts.

answer.text: They succeed exclusively on numerical calculation tasks and fail on all natural language processing.

feedback.text: Incorrect. LLMs excel at language tasks, but historical transcription requires faithful image-to-text fidelity.

answer.text: They are effective only when run on local microcontrollers without internet access.

feedback.text: Incorrect. Modern VLMs require substantial server infrastructure.

answer.text: They succeed at OCR post-correction while failing at translation.

feedback.text: Incorrect. Studies prove LLM post-correction degrades OCR quality, while translation of established text is effective.

questiontext.text: Under what specific condition does an automated transcription tool genuinely save scholarly labour in a human-in-the-loop workflow?

generalfeedback.text: Automation saves labour only below the threshold where correction costs less than transcription — and you have now measured where your tools sit.

answer.text: Only when the model's accuracy is high enough (e.g. CER below ~15%) that validating and correcting its output requires less time and cognitive effort than transcribing by hand.

feedback.text: Correct. If error rates exceed that threshold, post-correction is slower and more cognitively demanding than transcribing from scratch.

answer.text: Whenever the model is branded as an 'artificial intelligence' system.

feedback.text: Incorrect. Marketing labels do not alter empirical workflow economics.

answer.text: Only when the human transcriber is completely removed from the editorial loop.

feedback.text: Incorrect. Human verification remains essential for diplomatic fidelity; automation shifts labour to validation.

answer.text: Whenever the software is funded by an external university research grant.

feedback.text: Incorrect. Labour savings depend on empirical error rates and verification costs.

name.text: 16 Question: Documenting AI Use in the Repository

questiontext.text: Why is the Model-Access-Date trailer specifically necessary when documenting output generated by commercial hosted VLMs?

generalfeedback.text: Record the model access date — a hosted model can change without notice, making the date the only record of what produced the output.

answer.text: Hosted models can be updated or replaced behind an unchanging API endpoint without notice, making the date the only stable record of what system produced the text.

feedback.text: Correct. Unannounced backend model updates mean an experiment run in September may not be reproducible in December without the access date.

answer.text: To allow Git to automatically bill the user's credit card on the monthly anniversary.

feedback.text: Incorrect. Git trailers are text metadata for provenance, not billing mechanisms.

answer.text: Because hosted model licenses expire 24 hours after text generation.

feedback.text: Incorrect. Generated text does not expire, but model reproducibility requires date tracking.

answer.text: To ensure the commit complies with the Unicode Consortium's calendar specification.

feedback.text: Incorrect. Date tracking is a scholarly provenance requirement for ephemeral hosted APIs.

questiontext.text: When building the three-way comparison table (logs/three-way-w4.md), why must you specifically include lines containing uncertainty or physical damage?

generalfeedback.text: Compare on the lines where you recorded uncertainty — agreement on easy lines is uninformative, and divergence on hard lines is the finding.

answer.text: Agreement on clear, easy lines reveals little, whereas divergence on damaged or difficult lines exposes how each system behaves when visual evidence is ambiguous.

feedback.text: Correct. Hard lines highlight the contrast between human caution (<gap/>), HTR breakdown (impossible characters), and VLM hallucination (fluent invention).

answer.text: Because the TEI validator requires damaged lines to be highlighted in bold red text.

feedback.text: Incorrect. Markdown comparison tables are analytical research tools, not TEI validation scripts.

answer.text: To demonstrate that human transcribers make more errors on damaged text than vision-language models.

feedback.text: Incorrect. Human transcribers properly record gaps, whereas models tend to fabricate text.

answer.text: Because undamaged lines cannot be rendered in GitHub flavored markdown tables.

feedback.text: Incorrect. All lines can be rendered; damaged lines provide the most diagnostic evidence.

name.text: 18 Question: Error Taxonomy Across the Three

questiontext.text: What fundamental difference between specialized HTR and vision-language models is revealed by their error taxonomy?

generalfeedback.text: The VLM's distinctive failures are not recognition errors but consequences of being a language model — and the HTR model cannot make your expectation-driven errors.

answer.text: VLM failures (commentary, lost line breaks, fluent fabrication) are consequences of being a generative language model, whereas HTR models are bounded to ink and cannot make expectation-driven errors.

feedback.text: Correct. HTR errors are image-mapping failures, while VLM errors stem from imposing linguistic and conversational priors onto a reading task.

answer.text: Specialized HTR models make more formatting errors because they lack recurrent neural layers.

feedback.text: Incorrect. HTR models preserve line structure because they operate on segmented line images.

answer.text: Vision-language models make no errors on Greek abbreviations because their vocabulary is infinite.

feedback.text: Incorrect. VLMs frequently expand abbreviations silently or hallucinate expansions.

answer.text: Human transcribers never suffer from expectation bias when reading familiar literature.

feedback.text: Incorrect. Transcribers frequently suffer from expectation bias, which HTR models structurally avoid.

questiontext.text: Why is a carefully documented negative result (e.g. a VLM producing high CER and fabricating readings) valuable in scholarly digital humanities?

generalfeedback.text: A documented failure — this model, this prompt, this manuscript, this rate — is a contribution, and vague dismissal is not.

answer.text: It establishes an empirical boundary on what a specific tool can and cannot do on historical material, preventing future researchers from repeating the failure.

feedback.text: Correct. Transparent negative results with documented models, prompts, and error rates provide essential evidence for scholarly tool selection.

answer.text: It automatically qualifies the researcher for compensation from the AI software vendor.

feedback.text: Incorrect. Scientific reporting serves academic scholarship, not commercial vendor disputes.

answer.text: It proves that digital methods are fundamentally incompatible with all historical manuscripts.

feedback.text: Incorrect. It clarifies which specific tools are suitable for which specific palaeographical tasks.

answer.text: It allows the researcher to omit the methodology section from the final project report.

feedback.text: Incorrect. Documenting negative results requires thorough methodological reporting.

questiontext.text: Why must you explicitly reinstall and test your Git pre-commit hooks when working from a fresh clone during a remote session?

generalfeedback.text: Hooks are not cloned — install and test your NFC hook on this machine before committing anything today.

answer.text: Git hooks live in .git/hooks/ and are never copied during a clone or pull, so uninstalled hooks will silently fail to enforce NFC normalization.

feedback.text: Correct. Hooks are local to a clone; without manual installation from tools/, commits made on a remote machine can introduce decomposed NFD Greek.

answer.text: Fresh clones disable write permissions on all markdown files until a hook is compiled.

feedback.text: Incorrect. Git allows commits without hooks; the danger is silent loss of normalization enforcement.

answer.text: Git pre-commit hooks are automatically downloaded and executed by GitHub on push.

feedback.text: Incorrect. Pre-commit hooks run locally prior to commit creation, not remotely on GitHub.

answer.text: Transkribus will reject API calls originating from IP addresses without pre-commit hooks.

feedback.text: Incorrect. Transkribus has no knowledge of local client Git hooks.

name.text: 21 Question: What Wednesday and Friday Together Established

questiontext.text: What central thesis connects all empirical findings across Topic 4 (transfer learning, specialization gap, over-historicization, layout cascading)?

generalfeedback.text: Every finding in the table is a measurement against a hand-produced ground truth — which is the week's thesis in operation.

answer.text: Automated transcription accelerates workflow but fundamentally requires human diplomatic transcription as an authoritative baseline to measure, evaluate, and mitigate errors.

feedback.text: Correct. Every computational claim and error metric is a distance measured against an authoritative hand-produced ground truth.

answer.text: Neural networks have rendered human palaeographical expertise entirely obsolete for historical editing.

feedback.text: Incorrect. Automation amplifies human judgment, which remains necessary for ground truth and validation.

answer.text: Vision-language models will achieve 0% error rates on all medieval manuscripts once parameter counts exceed 1 trillion.

feedback.text: Incorrect. Parameter scale without domain exposure does not resolve the specialization gap.

answer.text: Digital editions should avoid all forms of automation to preserve traditional scholarly authority.

feedback.text: Incorrect. The thesis demonstrates how to integrate automation rigorously with human baseline controls.

questiontext.text: For a well-known classical or biblical text, which checklist verification item is most critical for detecting an unfaithful VLM transcription?

generalfeedback.text: For a well-known text, the memorization test is the most important check available — nothing else detects a recited printed edition.

answer.text: Testing for memorization at known variant reading locations and damaged lacunae.

feedback.text: Correct. A model reciting a standard printed edition from memory will produce beautiful output that completely falsifies the witness's unique textual evidence.

answer.text: Checking whether the file size of the raw output is an exact multiple of 64 bytes.

feedback.text: Incorrect. File size has no bearing on textual fidelity or memorization.

answer.text: Running a sentiment analysis classifier over the transcribed Greek prose.

feedback.text: Incorrect. Sentiment analysis is irrelevant to diplomatic transcription fidelity.

answer.text: Confirming that the VLM output contains no mentions of 21st-century technology.

feedback.text: Incorrect. The critical failure is subtle recitation of printed editions rather than overt anachronisms.

questiontext.text: What is the primary activity of Meeting #12 (Tuesday of Week 5) before quantitative CER and WER measurements are computed?

generalfeedback.text: Week 5 double-keys the ground truth and then measures against it — and the Transcription Assignment on October 2 includes the reconciliation report.

answer.text: Double-keying the manual ground truth to produce a verified consensus text by adjudicating differences between independent passes.

feedback.text: Correct. Double-keying refines the human ground truth so that machine outputs are scored against a truly accurate reference.

answer.text: Retraining the HTR model from scratch using a commercial supercomputer cluster.

feedback.text: Incorrect. Week 5 focuses on double-keying consensus and quantitative measurement.

answer.text: Deleting all raw machine outputs to save disk space in the Git repository.

feedback.text: Incorrect. Raw machine outputs must be preserved to compute error rates.

answer.text: Writing a grant proposal to license proprietary OCR software for the department.

feedback.text: Incorrect. Meeting #12 is an editorial consensus session.

name.text: 24 Question: What Good Work Looks Like Here

questiontext.text: What distinguishes a high-quality analysis of AI-assisted transcription in a digital edition report?

generalfeedback.text: A specific measured conclusion about your manuscript is the deliverable; a general claim about AI is a repetition of what you were told.

answer.text: Formulating a specific, measured conclusion about model performance on your particular manuscript rather than repeating general assertions about AI.

feedback.text: Correct. Scholarly digital editing requires grounded empirical findings (rates, failure types, specific hand behaviors) tailored to the witness.

answer.text: Claiming that the vision-language model performed flawlessly without checking the manuscript image.

feedback.text: Incorrect. Unchecked acceptance of fluent output is an uncritical failure.

answer.text: Writing an abstract philosophical essay on whether machines can truly 'read' literature.

feedback.text: Incorrect. The deliverable is an empirical, evidence-based assessment of tool performance.

answer.text: Relying entirely on published third-party benchmark figures without testing your own document.

feedback.text: Incorrect. Replicating measurements on your specific manuscript is the central objective.

name.text: 25 Question: A Note on Tool Choice for the Rest of the Term

questiontext.text: Based on Week 4's findings, how should you proceed if your fine-tuned HTR model achieves under 10% CER while your VLM exhibits high error and hallucinations?

generalfeedback.text: Let today's measurement set your tool choices for the term, and record the reasons at the time rather than reconstructing them later.

answer.text: Use the fine-tuned HTR model for primary transcription across remaining folios (correcting its output against images), and restrict VLM use to secondary tasks like translation and code drafting.

feedback.text: Correct. This applies the right tool to the right task based on measured empirical capabilities.

answer.text: Abandon HTR entirely and generate the rest of the edition using zero-shot VLM prompts.

feedback.text: Incorrect. Using a hallucinating tool for primary transcription destroys editorial fidelity.

answer.text: Pass the HTR output through the VLM to automatically correct spelling and grammar.

feedback.text: Incorrect. As established in Lesson 4.2 section 24, LLM post-correction degrades OCR quality.

answer.text: Transcribe the remaining 200 pages exclusively by hand without ever opening Transkribus again.

feedback.text: Incorrect. An HTR model under 10% CER is viable and saves significant labour in a human-in-the-loop workflow.

questiontext.text: Why does the three-step cycle (manual reference, deterministic tool, AI-assisted tool) generalize across digital humanities research?

generalfeedback.text: The three-step cycle is a general method for evaluating tools against material, and it collapses if the manual reference is compromised.

answer.text: It provides a structured comparative methodology for evaluating computational tools against specific materials, anchored by an independent human reference.

feedback.text: Correct. Comparing manual, bounded deterministic, and unbounded generative approaches reveals the true strengths and failure modes of each method.

answer.text: It is a legal framework mandated by international digital copyright treaties.

feedback.text: Incorrect. It is a scholarly and empirical evaluation method, not a legal treaty.

answer.text: It proves that automated algorithms will always outperform human domain specialists within three iterations.

feedback.text: Incorrect. The method often demonstrates where automation fails on complex cultural artifacts.

answer.text: It eliminates the need to validate XML schemas or maintain version-controlled repositories.

feedback.text: Incorrect. Strict validation and version control are essential pillars of the workflow.

questiontext.text: Why might manual transcription be more economical than HTR model training for an edition of a short passage (e.g. 25 lines)?

generalfeedback.text: For a short passage, HTR's setup cost may never amortize — say so if you find it, because the measurement is the point.

answer.text: The substantial setup cost of HTR (layout analysis, polygon correction, ground truth alignment, and training) may never amortize over a small number of lines.

feedback.text: Correct. HTR becomes cost-effective across large volumes of text, whereas a single short folio can be transcribed manually in less time than configuring an HTR pipeline.

answer.text: Because Transkribus charges a flat fee of $10,000 for any project with fewer than 50 lines.

feedback.text: Incorrect. Platform billing is credit-based per page, but human setup time is the major cost factor.

answer.text: Because manual transcription requires zero cognitive attention from the editor.

feedback.text: Incorrect. Manual transcription requires intense cognitive concentration, but zero toolchain setup overhead.

answer.text: Because HTR models cannot process text passages that contain fewer than 500 unique Greek words.

feedback.text: Incorrect. Models can process any length, but the human setup effort does not amortize on short texts.

questiontext.text: Why must Git tags created during Week 4 (e.g. vlm-w4-raw) be explicitly pushed with git push --tags?

generalfeedback.text: Push tags explicitly — they are not pushed by default, and Week 5's measurement retrieves the tagged states.

answer.text: Git does not push tags by default during a standard git push, and unpushed tags will be inaccessible on other machines during Week 5's measurement sessions.

feedback.text: Correct. Explicitly pushing tags ensures that repository snapshots are available across machines and to collaborators.

answer.text: Pushing tags automatically triggers a remote rebuild of the IIIF image server.

feedback.text: Incorrect. Git tags are repository references; they do not control remote IIIF image servers.

answer.text: Unpushed tags cause Git to automatically revert all commits created in the last 24 hours.

feedback.text: Incorrect. Commits remain safe on the branch, but unpushed tags remain local.

answer.text: Tags must be pushed to prevent GitHub from marking the repository as inactive.

feedback.text: Incorrect. Repository activity is determined by commits, but pushing tags is essential for sharing milestones.

questiontext.text: How do the findings of Tuesday (manual), Wednesday (HTR), and Friday (VLM) synthesize into a single cohesive argument?

generalfeedback.text: Three meetings, one thesis — automation accelerates transcription and depends absolutely on a hand-produced reference to be evaluated at all.

answer.text: Automation accelerates transcription but fundamentally requires a hand-produced diplomatic ground truth as an authoritative anchor to evaluate and interpret its outputs.

feedback.text: Correct. Neither bounded HTR nor generative VLMs can calibrate or validate themselves; human diplomatic transcription provides the essential measuring instrument.

answer.text: They demonstrate that computer vision should be completely replaced by statistical word embeddings.

feedback.text: Incorrect. The three steps evaluate complementary computational and manual methods.

answer.text: They show that all three methods produce identical character error rates on damaged Byzantine manuscripts.

feedback.text: Incorrect. The three methods exhibit drastically different error rates and error categories.

answer.text: They prove that historical manuscripts can be transcribed without ever looking at the physical parchment images.

feedback.text: Incorrect. High-resolution facsimile inspection is fundamental to all three stages.

name.text: 30 Question: Synthesis: Fluency Is Not Fidelity

questiontext.text: What is the overarching theoretical lesson of Topic 4 regarding generative AI in digital textual scholarship?

generalfeedback.text: Fluency and fidelity are independent, and the more plausible a tool's output, the less its plausibility tells you about its accuracy.

answer.text: Fluency and fidelity are independent properties; the more plausible and grammatical an automated model's output appears, the less its fluency guarantees accuracy against the historical source.

feedback.text: Correct. Generative models excel at linguistic fluency while disguising severe factual errors; fidelity can only be established by human verification against the artifact.

answer.text: Any text that is grammatically fluent in Greek is mathematically guaranteed to be historically accurate.

feedback.text: Incorrect. Grammatical fluency is an internal linguistic property that frequently disguises hallucinations.

answer.text: Generative AI models should only be evaluated on the basis of typography and font rendering.

feedback.text: Incorrect. Evaluation must focus on textual fidelity, character preservation, and error profiles.

answer.text: Conspicuous errors in specialized HTR models prove that statistical computing has no place in philology.

feedback.text: Incorrect. Conspicuous errors are advantageous because they are easily detected and corrected without deceiving the editor.
